author: high5
claim: If G has a matching M saturating X, then |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X.
evidence: For each x in S, the unique edge of M incident with x has its other endpoint in N(S). Distinct x in S have distinct matched endpoints because M is a matching. Thus x maps injectively to its M-partner in N(S), so |S| <= |N(S)|.

glossary.G: the finite bipartite graph in the problem
glossary.X: the left vertex class of G
glossary.Y: the right vertex class of G
glossary.N(S): the set of vertices of Y adjacent in G to at least one vertex of S

author: high5
claim: If a nonempty proper A subset X satisfies |N(A)|=|A|, then Hall's condition descends both to the induced graph on A and N(A), and to the induced graph on X\A and Y\N(A).
evidence: For T subseteq A, every neighbor of T lies in N(A), so its neighborhood in the first induced graph is N(T), of size at least |T|. For T subseteq X\A, the neighborhood in the second induced graph is N(T)\N(A). Since N(A union T)=N(A) disjoint union (N(T)\N(A)), Hall's inequality on A union T gives |A|+|N(T)\N(A)| >= |A|+|T|, hence |N(T)\N(A)| >= |T|.

glossary.X: the left vertex class of G
glossary.Y: the right vertex class of G
glossary.N(S): the set of vertices of Y adjacent in G to at least one vertex of S
glossary.A: a nonempty proper subset of X
glossary.T: a subset of A or of X\A, as specified

author: high
claim: If G has a matching saturating every vertex of X, then |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X.
evidence: Let M be such a matching. For each x in S, let m(x) be the endpoint in Y of the unique edge of M incident with x. Since M is a matching, x -> m(x) is injective; since m(x) is adjacent to x, m(x) lies in N(S). Thus S injects into N(S), so finiteness gives |S| <= |N(S)|.

links.statement: The matching condition implies Hall's neighborhood inequalities.

glossary.G: the finite bipartite graph in the problem
glossary.X: the left vertex class of G
glossary.Y: the right vertex class of G
glossary.N(S): the set of vertices in Y adjacent to at least one vertex of S
glossary.m(x): the vertex of Y matched to x by M

author: high6
claim: Any matching that saturates X forces |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X.
evidence: Let M be a matching saturating X. For any S subseteq X, the M-edges incident with vertices of S have pairwise distinct endpoints in Y, and every such endpoint lies in N(S). Thus N(S) contains |S| distinct vertices.

links.statement: The matching condition implies Hall's neighborhood inequalities.

author: high6
claim: The Hall inequalities are preserved in the two smaller graphs arising from the standard tight-set/strict-slack induction split.
evidence: If a nonempty proper A subset X has |N(A)|=|A|, then the graph on A and N(A) satisfies Hall directly, while for B=X\A the graph on B and Y\N(A) satisfies Hall because for T subset B, |N(A union T)|=|N(A)|+|N(T)\N(A)| >= |A|+|T|. If every nonempty proper A has |N(A)|>|A|, choose an edge xy and delete x,y; for nonempty T subset X\{x}, the new neighborhood has size at least |N(T)|-1 >= |T|.

links.statement: Induction reductions in both the tight-set and strict-slack cases satisfy Hall.

glossary.A: a nonempty proper subset of X
glossary.T: a subset of a smaller left vertex class

author: high2
claim: If a matching in G saturates X, then |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X.
evidence: For each x in S, let y_x be the Y-endpoint of the unique matching edge incident with x. Because a matching has no shared endpoints, the vertices y_x are pairwise distinct; each y_x lies in N(S). Thus x -> y_x is an injection from S into N(S), and finiteness gives |S| <= |N(S)|.

glossary.G: the finite bipartite graph with bipartition X and Y
glossary.N(S): the set of neighbors in Y of vertices of S
glossary.y_x: the Y-endpoint of the matching edge incident with x

author: high7
claim: If a matching of G saturates X, then |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X.
evidence: Let M saturate X. For each x in S, the unique edge of M incident with x has a right endpoint f(x) in N(S). Since distinct edges in a matching have disjoint endpoints, f(x) != f(x') whenever x != x'. Thus f is an injection S -> N(S), so finiteness gives |S| <= |N(S)|.

glossary.G: the finite bipartite graph under consideration
glossary.X: the left bipartition class of G
glossary.Y: the right bipartition class of G
glossary.N(S): the set of vertices of Y adjacent in G to at least one vertex of S

author: high3
claim: Necessity in Hall's theorem: if a finite bipartite graph G=(X sqcup Y,E) has a matching saturating X, then |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X.
evidence: For each x in X, let m(x) be the Y-endpoint of the unique matching edge incident with x. Distinct vertices of X have distinct images because no two edges in a matching share an endpoint, so m is injective. If S subseteq X, every m(x) with x in S is adjacent to x and hence lies in N(S). Thus m(S) subseteq N(S), while injectivity gives |m(S)|=|S|. Therefore |N(S)|>=|S|.

links.statement: If a matching saturates X, then Hall's inequalities hold.

glossary.N: the neighborhood operator on subsets of X
glossary.m: the map sending each left vertex to its partner in the matching
